- The data likely exhibited incomplete conversion (a plateau before substrate depletion), which reversible inhibition cannot fit well, but irreversible catalyst death can.
- The aim for the turn was achieved: we successfully ruled out M7 and isolated the specific class of irreversible deactivation mechanisms.

<hypothesis>
To distinguish between the remaining top deactivation models (M11, M14, M20, M17, M16), we must break the quasi-steady-state approximation (QSSA). Under standard conditions, models like M11 (deactivation via S + cat) and M14 (deactivation via catS) are mathematically very similar because [S][cat] is proportional to [catS]. 
By setting the initial substrate and catalyst concentrations to be equal and relatively low (S=0.2, cat=0.2), we enter a stoichiometric regime. In this regime, free S and free cat will rapidly bind and deplete each other to form the `catS` complex. 
- For M11 (S+cat), the deactivation rate will drop quadratically as free S and free cat are consumed.
- For M14 (catS), the deactivation rate will remain high and linear with respect to the complex.
- For M16 (S+catS), the deactivation rate will be extremely low because both S and catS are small fractions of 0.2.
- For M17 (P+catS), deactivation will be delayed and minimal because the maximum possible product formed is only 0.2, keeping P low throughout the reaction.
This single experiment will force these mathematically similar models to diverge significantly in their predicted kinetic trajectories.
</hypothesis>
